A.explanation: Far too small for a 3.20 s flight. It does not satisfy $u = gT/2$ with $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.

B.explanation: About half the required value. It results from halving the time to the top again, using only about $0.80 \text{ s}$ of deceleration.

C.explanation: Matches $u = g \times 1.60 \text{ s} = 15.7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, the speed removed by gravity during the upward half of the flight.

D.explanation: Twice the required value. It is $g \times 3.20 \text{ s}$ and treats the whole return time as the time to slow to zero.

hints: Notice that $3.20 \text{ s}$ is the total time to go up and come back to the hand, so the upward journey to zero velocity takes only part of that time.
With negligible air resistance the up and down motions are symmetric under acceleration $9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ downwards, so find the time from launch to the top where velocity is momentarily zero.
Apply $v = u + at$ to the upward part with $v = 0$ at the top and $a = -g$, then solve for the initial speed $u$ using the half-time in $\text{s}$.
walkthrough: Take upward as positive. For the whole $T = 3.20 \text{ s}$ flight the displacement back to the hand is zero and acceleration is $a = -g = -9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
By symmetry the ball takes half the total time to rise to its highest point where $v = 0$. So time up $t = T/2 = 3.20/2 = 1.60 \text{ s}$.
Use $v = u + at$ for the upward motion: $0 = u - g t$.
Substitute values with units: $u = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2} \times 1.60 \text{ s} = 15.696 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Check units and size: $\text{m s}^{-2} \times \text{s} = \text{m s}^{-1}$, about $15.7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ to three significant figures. This is option C
